editor_spans.body: Read past the 'double down' language and the sums are modest. The headline accelerated delivery is £10 million out of a £45 million missile package. The larger LMM commitment, £1.6 billion, is spread over four years. Britain can promise resolve 'for as long as it takes', but it cannot quickly produce air-defence munitions at the scale Russia's drone campaign demands.

Where Britain does have unusual weight is finance and shipping. The maritime services ban on Russian LNG and the push for partners to copy it rely on London's insurance and shipping markets, not its factories. Decades of building a service economy rather than an industrial one now shape how Britain fights a proxy war: by denying services, not by out-producing anyone.

The energy ceasefire is also not purely altruistic. The Prime Minister described it as the quickest way to get diesel back onto world markets. The government separately acknowledges that the conflict feeds through to energy prices and the cost of living. The diplomacy serves Ukraine, but it also serves British households.

The US-Russia agreement exposes Britain's position. London 'fully supports US-led efforts' while insisting on supporting Ukraine for as long as it takes. When Washington sets the terms, the UK's role is to keep Ukraine supplied and to hope the American framework holds.

Andy Burnham built his career as a metro mayor arguing against Whitehall centralism. As Prime Minister he is now pointing that argument at Holyrood, calling it one of Europe's most centralised devolved administrations.

The offer is not neutral. It would route regional empowerment through No10 North and the Scotland Office. That gives Westminster a direct relationship with Scottish cities and regions that partly bypasses the Scottish Government.

The same week shows a different instinct on rail. Great British Railways consolidates the network under one national public body. Putting its headquarters in Derby moves the building, not the control.

Taken together, the government favours devolution when it weakens a rival centre in Edinburgh and national ownership when it is the centre itself. Whether that is a coherent philosophy or a convenient one will become clear when English regions ask for a say over GBR.

The most consequential line in the Commons statement was not about the November summit's food and energy deals. It was the Prime Minister's call for a 'serious dialogue' about long-term options for the EU relationship, with 'the British public' as 'the boss'. That phrasing points toward a future public vote, even though no such vote is announced.

The stated gains are real but small. About £10 billion a year by 2040 is a minor share of a roughly £2.5–3 trillion economy. The concrete harms he lists include document checks on salmon, banned seed potatoes and £200 health certificates. These are the predictable costs of the 2020 settlement, which put sovereignty over market access.

'Britain is back' is presented as a statement about Britain's global standing. Underneath, it is an argument at home that the post-2016 settlement has run its course. The summit is the first test of whether voters will accept that framing.
